analysis.one_liner: Protects the land around Chaco Canyon in New Mexico from new oil, gas, and mining development.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill — it sat in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently remove federal land around Chaco Culture National Historical Park from new oil and gas leasing, mining, and other development. It would also terminate oil and gas leases on that land that have never produced fuel, while leaving already-producing operations and tribal mineral rights untouched. The Interior Department could hand or swap some of the protected land to Native tribes. The purpose is to shield a World Heritage Site, sacred sites, and nearby tribal communities from the drilling boom in the Mancos and Gallup shale formations.
analysis.who_benefits: Pueblo tribes, the Navajo Nation, and the Hopi Tribe, who use the Greater Chaco landscape for ceremony and consider it sacred; residents of nearby communities who live with the air, noise, and safety effects of extensive natural gas development; and visitors to the national park, whose experience of the landscape and night skies would be protected from new drilling [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribes and residents near Chaco Canyon

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws federal land within the Chaco Cultural Heritage Withdrawal Area from all new oil and gas leasing, mining claims, geothermal leasing, and disposal under public land laws [S3].
Automatically terminates oil and gas leases on that land that never began drilling and never produced in paying quantities, and the Secretary may not extend them [S3].
Allows the Interior Department to convey or exchange the withdrawn land to an Indian tribe under an approved resource management plan, putting protection decisions in tribal hands [S3].
Explicitly preserves tribal mineral rights on trust and allotment land and allows water, power, utility, and road improvements for communities adjacent to the withdrawn land [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding undeveloped leases in the area lose those leases, and companies hoping to drill the Mancos/Gallup shale lose access to the federal minerals. New Mexico also forgoes federal mineral royalties from the withdrawn acreage, revenue that helps fund state schools and services [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies with undeveloped leases

drawbacks.text: Terminating nonproducing leases and barring new development forfeits federal mineral royalties on the withdrawn land, revenue New Mexico uses for schools and public services [S3].
The withdrawal covers only federal land; drilling on nearby state, private, and tribal allotment land — a major source of local impacts — would continue under existing law [S3].
Companies holding valid leases in paying quantities keep their rights, so the protection is partial by design and depends on which leases were still nonproducing at enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — permanent protection of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, sacred sites, and community health around the park — is real but regional, and the bill deliberately leaves producing leases and tribal mineral rights alone. The cost is concentrated on leaseholders who never drilled and on forgone royalties. The tradeoff favors protection, though critics would fairly note the bill cannot stop development happening just outside its boundaries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill on May 2, 2023, joined by Sen. Martin Heinrich, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1].
The bill received one cosponsor and no further action after the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history [S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill was not reintroduced in that session, so no chamber ever voted on it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators holding undeveloped leases and companies interested in the Mancos/Gallup shale kept access to federal minerals around Chaco, and New Mexico kept the royalty stream. Tribes and nearby residents did not get the statutory protection the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas leaseholders near Chaco

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to withdraw federal land around Chaco Canyon from new oil, gas, and mining development.

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its other original sponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred; no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and gas operators in the San Juan Basin
against.role: Leaseholders and developers in the Mancos/Gallup shale play
against.what_they_did: Opposed permanent withdrawal of federal minerals around Chaco, which would terminate nonproducing leases and block future leasing.

sides.party_line_note: Only the two Democratic senators from New Mexico sponsored the bill and its single cosponsor was a Democrat; it never reached a vote, so there is no record of how Republicans or the full chamber would have voted [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers in the San Juan Basin (Mancos/Gallup shale)
industries.note: The bill terminates nonproducing federal leases around Chaco and bars all new leasing there, cutting off drilling near the park. The bill's own findings tie extensive natural gas development to harms to the health, safety, economies, and quality of life of nearby tribal communities, so the industry's gain from blocking the bill came at those communities' expense.
The withdrawn land would also be closed to mining claims and geothermal leasing. This is a minor effect for this area compared with oil and gas.
